evidence.section_title: Life on the Seesaw: A Qualitative Study of Suicide Resiliency Factors for Young Gay Men
evidence.quote: Using grounded theory methodology, we explored the suicide resiliency in eight young gay men in Aotearoa/New Zealand.

[page/6/Text/5] Interested participants were asked in a pre-interview discussion whether they had ever attempted suicide before. Persons who indicated that they had attempted suicide were then asked if they felt psychologically and emotionally able to discuss the event without causing themselves undue distress and pain. None of the volunteers decided to withdraw. After four attempters and four non-attempters volunteered to participate, sampling finished. Equal numbers of attempters and non-attempters were interviewed so as to provide a range of experiences for analysis.

Commenting on a "gay hour" provided by student radio, Tim illustrates that such programmes can not only directly help reduce a sense of isolation and alienation, but can also inform L/B/G youth about support organisations: . . . So I definitely knew that there were things out there which would provide opportunities, it wasn't like I felt like, you know, there's no where to go now and I'm all stuck by myself. (Tim, 20, non-attempter) Carl's testimony impresses how necessary role models of the same ethnicity can be to L/B/G youth. Such role models may provide points to identify with that are consistent with their cultural identities as well as their L/B/G identities: Irirangi Teakiawa, he's like a really awesome, he was like the best, the bombest, um Taiaha, he was really really awesome . . . he's like, the man at doing Taiaha, and Patu and everything, and that he wasn't quite straight, so he was a really big role model. . . . And because he's kind of like, he's kind of in my tribe kind of thing, he definitely is a big idle of mine, . . . especially being Maori. He's Maori, and he was queer, and he was the bomb at doing this and I really appreciate that he came-out just before he died. (Carl, 18, attempter)

evidence.section_title: Life on the Seesaw: A Qualitative Study of Suicide Resiliency Factors for Young Gay Men
evidence.quote: Using grounded theory methodology, we explored the suicide resiliency in eight young gay men in Aotearoa/New Zealand.
[page/6/Text/5] Qualitative data were collected from in-depth 1- to 2-hour interviews.

The text contains direct quotes from participants identified by age and suicide experience (e.g., '(Tim, 20, non-attempter)', '(Carl, 18, attempter)', '(Sam, 19, non-attempter)'), indicating primary data collection through interviews.

evidence.section_title: Life on the Seesaw: A Qualitative Study of Suicide Resiliency Factors for Young Gay Men
evidence.quote: While considerable research has highlighted the factors that increase gay youth suicide risk, there has been much less emphasis on protective factors. Using grounded theory methodology, we explored the suicide resiliency in eight young gay men in Aotearoa/New Zealand. Common themes emerged, including positive social norms and conditions, high levels of support, identification with role models and high self-esteem. These were integrated with "known" risk factors to form the Seesaw Model of Gay Male Suicide. This model demonstrates that the balance between risk and resiliency may be the key to gay suicide.

The positive portrayal of L/G/B people and issues in mass media may help reduce feelings of invisibility, alienation and social isolation for L/B/G youth. Positive representations in the mass media were well known to Zac, who upon realising he was gay, reported being quite elated at the prospect of being able to be part of the "bisexual chic" noveau that was highly regarded in fashion magazines of the time. Positive media images of L/B/G people may be particularly important for young gay and bisexual men who do not know anyone who openly identifies as L/B/G. Commenting on a "gay hour" provided by student radio, Tim illustrates that such programmes can not only directly help reduce a sense of isolation and alienation, but can also inform L/B/G youth about support organisations: . . . So I definitely knew that there were things out there which would provide opportunities, it wasn't like I felt like, you know, there's no where to go now and I'm all stuck by myself. (Tim, 20, non-attempter) Carl emphasised how positive mass media portrayal (in the form of the locally produced Queer Nation television programme) may be an even more vital information source for rural-based youth who otherwise receive little positive information about L/B/G sexualities and possible support groups. Sam also found that positive mass media representations were beneficial during coming-out, because they directly tackled the negative stereotypes that he had of L/B/G people: Ian Roberts was good, because I can remember looking at him, and you know growing up gay you have a negative view of what a gay man is, even from when I was quite young I sort of had this vision of this old man, like an effeminate old man in a room alone with a suitcase and stuff (laugh) this was my vision of what a gay man was. But Ian Roberts being quite a masculine, league player figure, he was quite important just for breaking stereotypes. (Sam, 19, non-attempter) The influence of positive representations in the media was also high-lighted by Leon who commented that the positive portrayal of two gay characters on the national television soap opera Shortland Street were pivotal for him. As mass media both mirrors dominant societal ideologies and cultivates common values and outlooks (Gross, 1991), positive media images may also play a vital role in the formation of more general positive societal attitudes towards L/B/G people. These attitudes may in turn help create an environment more accepting to L/B/G young men who are in the process of coming out. Many L/B/G young people may also find positive role models in people that are part of their everyday lives. Tim detailed how his straight brother's friendship with an openly gay man helped reduce his own feelings of social isolation and how important it was to be shown the possibility of a gay man living a happy, fulfilling life: ... I knew there were stable gay people out there who lead full on lifestyles, and that they could be out and happy, and live like that and not be closeted. ... like it provides you with an option, and, and um, a role model that you know, that there is something out there that you can live that lifestyle. ... (Tim, 20, non-attempter) Carl's testimony impresses how necessary role models of the same ethnicity can be to L/B/G youth. Such role models may provide points to identify with that are consistent with their cultural identities as well as their L/B/G identities: Irirangi Teakiawa, he's like a really awesome, he was like the best, the bombest, um Taiaha, he was really really awesome . . . he's like, the man at doing Taiaha, and Patu and everything, and that he wasn't quite straight, so he was a really big role model. . . . And because he's kind of like, he's kind of in my tribe kind of thing, he definitely is a big idle of mine, . . . especially being Maori. He's Maori, and he was queer, and he was the bomb at doing this and I really appreciate that he came-out just before he died. (Carl, 18, attempter) For L/B/G members of nondominant ethinic groups, who often face the dual discrimination of racism and heterosexism (Erwin, 1993; Savin-Williams & Rodriguez, 1993; Schneider et al., 1989), such role models may be invaluable in proving one can be both "queer" and Maori.

[page/13/Text/4] In addition to the assistance Victor received from his teacher, he also indicated that he received significant support from other L/B/G friends. The support that L/B/G youth are able to give each other may have special importance due to a sense of shared experience. [page/13/Text/6] L/G/B friendships can further help to assist resiliency by providing a forum to enable L/B/G youth to collectively find solutions to their common problems. For example, by joining a L/B/G support group, Sam was helped to gain the knowledge he needed to address his problems and strengthen self-esteem: [page/13/Text/7] I went to "Ice Breakers" which was really good, which was a major step, sort of like reclaim self esteem, like up until that point I had never met an openly gay person, you know it was a pretty major thing at 16, um, and that was just really good meeting other young gay people, and we talked a lot, and I read a lot of books and got a lot of information that just wasn't given to me, and that was just the turning point. (Sam, 19, non-attempter) [page/13/Text/8] Not only may support groups serve to "normalise" L/B/G sexualities, but they may also provide youth with role models of other young men who have traversed the various tasks of coming-out to reach positive resolutions. [page/13/Text/9] Support networks may also offer respite from hostile home environments by providing L/B/G youth with somewhere to stay during diffi- [page/14/Text/2] cult periods. In some cases this may prevent a life on the streets and the danger of a negative spiral that may include drugs and prostitution (Kruks, 1991). Indeed, all participants in the current study reported that after time and space (which varied from 1 week to 5 months) away from other family members, the family and young people often become comfortable with the idea of living together again. [page/14/Text/3] Another role played by such support structures in the development of resiliency factors for L/B/G youth, lies in their ability to provide safe sex information (see Kegeles, Hays, & Coates, 1996). Various participants reported fears around HIV/AIDS infection, and Carl demonstrates that such fears and associated suicide risk could be reduced by sexually transmitted infections (STIs) education: [page/14/Text/4] I kind of had an HIV scare, not so long ago, I sort of thought I was HIV positive and if I was going to be HIV positive, I was, there was no question I just was going to do it . . . I was going to hurt myself, I just couldn't think of it any other way, because I just didn't want my family to see me like this, I didn't want them to see me like that. ...I just did not want to live if I had HIV, lack of education, I wasn't educated about the subject, I kind of thought about AIDS um ...I love my nieces and nephews and am I still going to be able to play with them, and stuff, if I can't play with my younger generation then I just don't want to be a part of their lives at all . . . but that was then, I know a lot more now . . . once I got the negative statement, and she [the doctor] like totally educated me, and I was like oh okay. (Carl, 19, attempter)

While some L/B/G youth like Leon and Sam appear to thrive during the coming-out process, the existing research literature cautions that many others face a coming-out process fraught with stressors. Differences in suicidality may not lie exclusively in the stress experienced by one person relative to another, but rather in the amount of resiliency afforded to them at that particular time. Positive societal acceptance may be the most influential resiliency factor available to L/B/G youth. The model recognises that L/B/G youth often carry the burden of various suicide risk factors, and that increasing resiliency factors may help swing the finely balanced seesaw away from a suicide attempt. However, the model also acknowledges the potential for risk factors to intensify at any point in time and the young person may once again tilt back towards a suicide attempt. To reflect this, the Seesaw Model includes factors at multiple levels of analysis that interact with each other; those that are best seen as reflecting societal norms and conditions (e.g., heterosexism and social isolation or positive societal acceptance, positive L/B/G representations, and support groups); the individual differences that concern the immediate social context of the young person (e.g., an early age at coming-out, rejection, depression, internalised homophobia, HIV knowledge, and bullying or family, peer and school support, availability of role models, and high self-esteem); and the various coping mechanisms (e.g., social withdrawal, and substance abuse or role model identification, and support seeking).
